clinicalPearls: The neurohypophysis releases arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH) and oxytocin from axons whose cell bodies sit in the hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei; AVP conserves water by concentrating urine, while oxytocin drives milk letdown and socioemotional behaviors (Harrison 22e p.3014).

AVP secretion is governed mainly by an osmotic set point in anteromedial hypothalamic osmoreceptors, with the average threshold near a plasma osmolality of ~275 mosmol/L and sodium ~135 meq/L; only a 2-4% rise above this drives maximum antidiuresis (Harrison 22e p.3015).

Nausea/emetic stimuli are extremely potent AVP releasers, producing 50- to 100-fold increases even without vomiting, far exceeding osmotic stimulation; AVP is also released by a >10-20% fall in blood pressure or volume, hypoglycemia, glucocorticoid deficiency, and smoking (Harrison 22e p.3015).

AVP acts on V2 receptors of collecting-duct principal cells to insert aquaporin-2 water channels, enabling water reabsorption; maximum antidiuresis (urine osmolality up to ~1200 mosmol/L) occurs at plasma AVP of roughly 1-3 pg/mL (Harrison 22e p.3016).
The thirst osmostat is set about 3% higher than the AVP osmostat, so antidiuresis is the first-line defense and thirst/polydipsia only engage once AVP's capacity is exceeded (Harrison 22e p.3016).

Polyuria-polydipsia is defined practically by a 24-h urine volume exceeding ~40-50 mL/kg and/or >3 L/d on unrestricted intake; dehydration and hypernatremia are uncommon in diabetes insipidus unless thirst or access to water is also impaired (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017).

Serum sodium at presentation is a key discriminator: a low sodium (<135 mmol/L) points toward primary polydipsia (patients can drink into hyponatremia), whereas a high sodium suggests AVP deficiency or resistance (Harrison 22e p.3017).

Copeptin, the stable C-terminal fragment of the AVP prohormone, has largely replaced direct AVP assays: a baseline copeptin >21.4 pmol/L without prior water deprivation identifies AVP resistance, and a copeptin >4.9 pmol/L at plasma sodium >=150 mmol/L after hypertonic saline distinguishes AVP deficiency from primary polydipsia with ~96.5% accuracy (Harrison 22e p.3017-3018).

The MRI posterior pituitary bright spot reflects AVP-containing neurosecretory vesicles and is often absent in AVP deficiency, but its absence is not diagnostic since it can persist early or be absent in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.3018).

In pregnancy, placental N-terminal aminopeptidase (vasopressinase) accelerates AVP clearance three- to fourfold, producing gestational AVP deficiency that typically remits weeks after delivery; the synthetic analogue DDAVP resists this peptidase (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017).

Hypoosmolality is the hallmark of SIAD; acute or severe hyponatremia can cause headache, confusion, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and coma, while even mild chronic hyponatremia raises the risk of falls, fractures, neurocognitive symptoms, and mortality (Harrison 22e p.3019).

In SIAD, persistent water retention modestly expands total body water and triggers compensatory urinary sodium loss, so edema does not develop; the harm comes from intracellular (notably cerebral) swelling proportional to the speed and degree of the sodium fall (Harrison 22e p.3019).
harrison.pathophysiology: Disorders of the neurohypophysis arise from deficient or excessive AVP secretion/action. In AVP deficiency (formerly central/neurogenic diabetes insipidus) and AVP resistance (formerly nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), impaired urine concentration increases free-water excretion, causing a small (1-2%) reduction in body water and a rise in plasma osmolality/sodium that stimulates thirst and compensatory drinking; severity ranges from near-complete deficiency unresponsive to maximal stimuli to partial defects in which mild stimuli can still partially concentrate urine, though prior lack of AVP transiently blunts renal concentrating capacity. Central deficiency reflects destruction or dysfunction of AVP-producing neurons (trauma, tumors, vascular, granulomatous, infectious, autoimmune/IgG4 hypophysitis, or genetic AVP-neurophysin II mutations); resistance reflects reduced renal V2-receptor/aquaporin-2 responsiveness from drugs (lithium), hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, infiltrative or vascular disease, or AVPR2/AQP2 mutations. Primary polydipsia is the mirror image: excess intake lowers plasma osmolality, physiologically suppresses AVP, and produces a dilute compensatory diuresis. Hypodipsic/adipsic hypernatremia results from anterior hypothalamic osmoreceptor damage impairing osmotic thirst (occasionally from anti-subfornical-organ autoantibodies), so obligatory renal/insensible losses go unreplaced. In SIAD, AVP is inappropriately elevated when it should be osmotically suppressed, causing water retention, slight volume expansion with renal sodium loss (no edema), and dilutional hypoosmolality with cellular swelling (Harrison 22e p.3014-3019).
additionalDifferentials: Complete vs partial central AVP deficiency
Nephrogenic AVP resistance (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, AVPR2/AQP2 mutations)
Primary (dipsogenic, psychogenic, compulsive, or health-enthusiast) polydipsia
Gestational AVP deficiency from placental vasopressinase
Pseudohyponatremia (hyperlipidemia, hyperproteinemia) and translocational hyponatremia (hyperglycemia, mannitol) as non-hypotonic mimics of SIAD
Hypovolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia (heart failure, cirrhosis, GI losses, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency)
infectionMimics: Meningitis, encephalitis, and tuberculosis affecting the hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal axis (causes of AVP deficiency)
Cytomegalovirus encephalitis and AIDS-related hypothalamic involvement causing adipsic hypernatremia
nonInfectiousMimics: Osmotic diuresis from diabetes mellitus mimicking diabetes insipidus polyuria
Pseudohyponatremia and translocational hyponatremia mimicking SIAD
Secondary adrenal insufficiency and (rarely) hypothyroidism presenting with hyponatremia
additionalInvestigations: 24-h urine volume on unrestricted fluids (>40-50 mL/kg/day and/or >3 L/d defines significant polyuria)
Serum sodium and plasma osmolality with paired urine osmolality
Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin (>4.9 pmol/L at sodium >=150 mmol/L favors AVP deficiency over primary polydipsia)
Baseline copeptin (>21.4 pmol/L identifies AVP resistance)
Desmopressin challenge to separate AVP deficiency from AVP resistance
Water deprivation test (older indirect gold standard, limited accuracy)
MRI of sella/suprasellar region including pituitary stalk and posterior pituitary bright spot
Urine sodium (<30 mmol/L suggests low effective arterial blood volume rather than SIAD)
Exclusion of adrenal insufficiency and assessment of thyroid function in hyponatremia workup
redFlags: Severe or acute hyponatremia with headache, confusion, vomiting, seizures, or coma (cerebral edema)
Hypernatremia with signs of hypovolemia (tachycardia, postural hypotension, azotemia) in adipsic patients
Denial of thirst or failure to drink when conscious and hypernatremic (virtually diagnostic of adipsia)
Rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, or thromboembolic disease complicating hypertonic dehydration
Polyuria with rising serum sodium signaling inadequate water replacement
Lithium use with persistent polyuria suggesting drug-induced AVP resistance
harrison.prognosis: Uncomplicated AVP deficiency is generally well managed with vasopressin replacement, restoring normal water balance. Hyponatremia is the most common complication of replacement and ranges from mild to severe. AVP resistance is difficult to treat and may respond only partially. Adipsic/hypodipsic hypernatremia carries higher risk because the absent thirst sensation predisposes to recurrent hypertonic dehydration and complications such as rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, and thromboembolism; long-term structured fluid-balance management is needed to prevent recurrence. In SIAD, even mild chronic hyponatremia is associated with increased falls, fractures, neurocognitive and neuromuscular symptoms, and increased morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.3017-3019).
pitfalls: Low basal AVP/V2 stimulation (e.g., in primary polydipsia) transiently blunts renal concentrating capacity, so the urine osmolality rise after exogenous AVP can falsely suggest a concentrating defect, undermining the traditional indirect water deprivation test (accuracy only ~70%, and ~41% in primary polydipsia) (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017).
Measurement of plasma AVP or copeptin has no diagnostic value in SIAD itself; copeptin is used for the polyuria differential, not for confirming SIAD (Harrison 22e p.3020).
Failing to measure serum osmolality risks misclassifying pseudohyponatremia or translocational hyponatremia as true hypotonic SIAD (Harrison 22e p.3019-3020).
Clinical assessment of volume status is inaccurate, so relying on examination alone to classify hyponatremia can mislead (Harrison 22e p.3020).
Secondary adrenal insufficiency must be excluded before diagnosing SIAD in euvolemic hyponatremia (Harrison 22e p.3020).
Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin testing requires close sodium monitoring; absence of the MRI bright spot is not by itself sufficient to diagnose AVP deficiency (Harrison 22e p.3018).
Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia or hypernatremia is dangerous; serum sodium must be corrected slowly with close monitoring (Harrison 22e p.3019-3020).
harrison.severityClassification: Diabetes insipidus is graded as complete versus partial AVP deficiency, and complete versus partial AVP resistance, distinguished by copeptin response, desmopressin response, and the magnitude of urine osmolality change. Hyponatremia severity is gauged by plasma sodium and tempo: severe/acute hyponatremia with neurologic symptoms warrants urgent treatment, whereas gradual or mild hyponatremia may be paucisymptomatic; replacement-related hyponatremia is categorized as mild (sodium 131-134 mmol/L) or more severe (<130 mmol/L). Hypernatremia severity in adipsic patients varies widely and correlates with hypovolemic complications (Harrison 22e p.3017-3019).
management: Desmopressin replacement is the mainstay for AVP deficiency (central diabetes insipidus), titrated to symptoms and urine output
Ensure adequate free-water access and encourage drinking to thirst to prevent hypernatraemia
For AVP resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) withdraw offending drugs and use a low-salt, low-protein diet with thiazide diuretics and amiloride or NSAIDs
Treat the underlying cause where present, such as a tumour, granulomatous, or autoimmune hypophysitis
Monitor serum sodium closely, since hyponatraemia is the commonest complication of desmopressin therapy
Manage adipsic or hypodipsic patients with a fixed fluid prescription and regular weight and sodium monitoring
Arrange specialist endocrine follow-up with pituitary imaging
